Included with: μὴ οὐ is used of an apprehended negative: / __I with finite forms of the Verb, after Verbs expressing fear or apprehension [{compare (μή 5th c.BC: Bacchylides Lyricus 8):}] / __I.a mostly with subjunctive, δείδω μὴ οὔ τίς τοι ὑπόσχηται τόδε ἔργον [{8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 10.39, compare 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.9, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.53, 57, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Meno” 89d, etc.: after historical tenses, with _optative_, ἠθύμησάν τινες ἐννοούμενοι μὴ οὐκ ἔχοιεν ὁπόθεν λαμβάνοιεν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 3.5.3, etc.}]: with future optative representing future indicative in indirect speech, μὴ οὐκ ὀρθῶς αὐτὸ ποιήσοις [{5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthyphro” 15d.}] / __I.b with indicative, ὁρᾶτε μὴ οὐκ ἐμοὶ μάλιστα τῶν πολιτῶν προσήκει [{5th-6th c.BC: Andocides Orator 1.103, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Laches” 196c, Alcaeus2.139d.}] / __I.2 without introductory Verb, with subjunctive, μή νύ τοι οὐ χραίσμῃ [{8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.28, compare 566, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Troades” 982}]; also to suggest hesitation, perhaps [{compare (μή 5th c.BC: Bacchylides Lyricus 9), μὴ οὐ τοῦτο ᾖ τὸ χρηστήριον 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.79, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 67b, “Smp.” 194c, 214c, etc.: also with _indicative_, μὴ τοῦτο οὐ καλῶς ὡμολογήσαμεν [prev. author] “Men.” 89c.}] / __I.3 μή is sometimes doubled, irregularly, for μὴ οὐ, ἐθαύμαζε δ᾽ εἴτις.. φοβοῖτο, μὴ ὁ γενόμενος καλὸς κἀγαθὸς.. μὴ τὴν μεγίστην χάριν ἔχοι [{5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.2.7, compare 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.13.}] / __II after a negative expressed or implied: / __II.1 with infinitive, / __II.1.a after Verbs of hindering, denying, avoiding, needing, when these Verbs are themselves negatived or questioned, οὐκέτι ἀνεβάλλοντο μὴ οὐ τὸ πᾶν μηχανήσασθαι they no longer hesitated to try every expedient, [{5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.88, compare 8.100, 119}]; τί δῆτα μέλλεις μὴ οὐ γεγωνίσκει; [{4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 627, compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 540, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 320, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.4.2, 4.3.8, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthydemus” 304c, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 24.24; G3762	οὐθείς	outheis		none	οὐθείς, οὐθέν, / later form for οὐδείς, οὐδέν, found in Attic dialect Inscrr. from 4th c.BC onwards along with οὐδείς, which it supersedes entirely from about 4th c.BC to 2nd c.BC (forty examples of θ, none of δ); οὐθείς is in a majority in Ptolemaic papyri up to about 2nd c.BC, after which οὐδείς begins to be common, but does not prevail until 1st c.AD; the evidence of non-Attic dialect Inscrr. is in general agreement with the {οὐθατόεις}; codices of [{5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus, 5th c.BC: Antipho Orator, 5th-6th c.BC: Andocides Orator, 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator, and 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus never have οὐθείς}], but the θ forms are frequently in those of [{5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus, 5th-6th c.BC: Isocrates Orator, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator, 4th c.BC: Hyperides Orator, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus, and 4th-3rd c.BC: Theophrastus Philosophus}], frequently as variants for the δ forms; also in Hellenistic writers, [{3rd c.BC: Teles Philosophus, 2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus, etc.}]; the frequency of θ forms in the uncials of [{LXX varies roughly according to the date (known or probable)}] of the translation of the book in question (though the δ forms are in a large majority in the [{LXX as a whole)}]; the θ forms are rare in codices of [{1st c.BC-1st c.AD: Strabo Geographus}] and later writers.

G3778	ταύταις	tautais	G:PRT	hence	οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο, / genitive τούτου, ταύτης, τούτου, etc.: the dual feminine never in Attic dialect, see ὁ, ἡ, τό, [near the start]:—demonstrative pronoun, this, common from [{8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus downwards}] / __A ORIGIN and FORMS: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο probably arose from a reduplication of the demonstrative ὁ, ἡ, τό with insertion of -υ- (= Sanskrit Particle u), e.g. ταῦτα from τα-υ-τα: Doric dialect genitive singular feminine τούτας [{5th-6th c.BC: Philolaus Philosophus 11; _nominative_ _plural_ τοῦτοι, ταῦται 2nd c.AD: Apollonius Dyscolus Grammaticus “de Syntaxi;” 111.23: the former occurs 5th c.BC: Sophron Comicus 24, “GDI” 3045 B 6 (from Selinus), “SIG” 339.16 (Rhodes, 3rd c.BC)}], etc., the latter is uncertain in [{5th c.BC: Sophron Comicus 97, certain in “SIG” 241 B 117 (Delph., 4th c.BC): in _Boeotian dialect_ all forms begin with οὑτ-}], as genitive singular neuter οὕτω [{“Supp.epigram” 3.359.11 (3rd c.BC)}]; accusative singular feminine οὕταν [{6th c.BC: Corinna Lyrica “Supp.” 2.80; _accusative_ _plural_ _neuter_ οὗτα “SIG” 1185.20 (Tanagra, 3rd c.BC), etc.: _genitive_ _plural_ _feminine_ _Attic dialect_ τούτων, Cretan dialect ταυτᾶν “Leg.Gort.” 5.19; _neuter_ ταύτων “Michel” 1334.10 (Elis, 4th c.BC).—In _Ionic dialect_ sometimes written ταότην, ταο̄τα, “SIG” 283.19 (Chios, 4th c.BC), 46.7 (Halic., 5th c.BC), +others}] —In _Attic dialect_ οὗτος was frequently strengthened by the _demonstrative_ -ί, οὑτοσί, αὑτηί, τουτί, _genitive_ τουτουί, _dative_ τουτῳί, _accusative_ τουτονί; plural nominative οὑτοιί, neuter ταυτί, etc., this man here: sometimes a Particle is inserted between the pronoun and -ί, as αὑτηγί for αὑτηί γε, [{5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 784}]; G3778	τούτοις	toutois	G:D	to these	οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο, / genitive τούτου, ταύτης, τούτου, etc.: the dual feminine never in Attic dialect, see ὁ, ἡ, τό, [near the start]:—demonstrative pronoun, this, common from [{8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus downwards}] / __A ORIGIN and FORMS: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο probably arose from a reduplication of the demonstrative ὁ, ἡ, τό with insertion of -υ- (= Sanskrit Particle u), e.g. ταῦτα from τα-υ-τα: Doric dialect genitive singular feminine τούτας [{5th-6th c.BC: Philolaus Philosophus 11; In Compos. with a transitive Verb σύν may refer to the Object as well as the Subject, as συγκατακτείνειν may mean kill one person as well as another, or, join with another in killing. / __D.I.2 of the completion of an action, altogether, completely, as in συνάγνυμι, συνασκέω 2, συνθρύπτω, συγκόπτω, συμπατέω, συμπληρόω, συντελέω, συντέμν; sometimes, therefore, it seems only to strengthen the force of the simple word. / __D.I.3 joined with numerals, σύνδυο two together, which sense often becomes distributive, by twos, two and two; so σύντρεις, σύμπεντε, etc., like Latin bini, terni, etc. / __D.II σύν in Compos., before β μ π φ ψ, becomes συμ-; before γ κ ξ Χ, συγ-; before λ συλ-; before σ usually συσ-; but becomes συ- before σ followed by a consonant (e.g. συστῆναι), before ζ, and perhaps sometimes before ξ. A, as an enclitic, it stands second word in the sentence, clause, or phrase, regardless of the meaning: ἐγγύθι τε Πριάμοιο καὶ Ἕκτορος near both Priam and Hector, [{8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 6.317; ἡμέτεραί τ᾽ ἄλοχοι καὶ νήπια τέκνα 2.136, compare 4.505, 7.295; αἰεί τε δὴ νηλὴς οὺ καὶ θράσους πλέως 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 42 codices, compare 291 (_anapaest meter_); ἄνευ τε δόλου καὶ ἀπάτης 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.69; ὑπέρ τε σοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀδελφῆς “PEnteux.” 6.6 (3rd c.BC)}]; τοῖς τε πόνοις καὶ μαθήμασι [{5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 537a, compare “Ti.” 70b; hence in 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Orestes” 897 πόλεος must be taken with what precedes (Porson (at [prev. work]))}]: but article + noun, preposition + noun are frequently regarded as forming a unity indivisible by τε, τοῖς κτανοῦσί τε [{4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Choephori” 41 (Lyric poetry); πρὸς βίαν τε [prev. author] “Pr.” 210}]; also the order is frequently determined by the meaning, τε being placed immediately after the word (or first word of a phrase or clause) which it joins to what precedes or to what follows, πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε [{8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.544; ἔξω δόμων τε καὶ πάτρας 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 665}]; the copulative or preparatory τε precedes many other particles, e.g. τε γάρ, τ᾽ ἄρα, τέ τις. / __D.2 τε is enclitic in signfs. B, C also, and stands early in its sentence, clause, or phrase (see. above), but many particles which follow τε in signf. A precede it in signfs. B, C, e.g. in signfs. B, C we have δέ τε, μέν τε, γάρ τε, ἀλλά τε, δ᾽ ἄρα τε, ὅς ῥά τε, οὔτ᾽ ἄρ τε, καὶ γάρ τίς τε, ὅς τίς τε, καί τε. / __E Etymology: signf. A is found also in Sanskrit ca, Latin -que; for signfs. B and c cf.
